## Purpose

Every other result in this package is generated by our own simulation
framework, in which the miscalibration is injected deliberately and so is
known by construction. That is the right way to validate the metrics, but it
cannot show that they say anything useful about an estimator somebody else
wrote. This vignette therefore scores a genuinely external, widely used
estimator — `EpiEstim`'s renewal-equation estimate of the instantaneous
reproduction number — against a ground truth it never sees.

The design deliberately avoids real surveillance data. For $R_t$ there is no
observable ground truth in a real outbreak, so a real dataset would let us
measure disagreement but not calibration. A deterministic SIR model gives an
exact $R_t$ trajectory, and the only stochasticity is in the observation
process, which is where a forecast evaluation metric should be looking.

The experiment sweeps **epidemic size**. The same epidemic curve is realised
in populations spanning two and a half orders of magnitude, so the
signal-to-noise ratio available to the estimator varies continuously while
the shape of the thing being estimated does not. The question is whether the
PIT-Wasserstein metrics track the estimator's dispersion calibration across
that range, and whether they say anything a proper score does not.

## 1. Simulation setup

We use a simple SIR model with known reproductive number dynamics. The true $R_t$ at each time point is analytically known:

$$R_t = R_0 \cdot \frac{S_t}{N}$$

The model is solved as a deterministic ODE on the proportion scale with
$R_0 = 2$, $\gamma = 1/5$ (a five-day infectious period) and a seed of
$10^{-4}$, over 100 days. Because $S_t$ is deterministic, $R_t = R_0 S_t$ is
exact at every time point: this is the ground truth against which `EpiEstim`
is scored. The incidence curve $\beta S_t I_t$ is the expected number of new
infections per capita per day, and is what the observation process below is
built on.

```{r}

sir_model = function(t, R0, g) {
  
  init <- c(S=1-1e-4, I=1e-4, R=0)
  parameters <- c(beta=R0 * g, gamma=g)
  time <- seq(0,t,length.out = t+1)
  
  eqn <- function(time,state,parameters){
    with(as.list(c(state,parameters)),{
      dS <- -beta*S*I
      dI <- beta*S*I-gamma*I
      dR <- gamma*I
      return(list(c(dS,dI,dR)))})
  }
  out = deSolve::ode(y=init,times=time,eqn,parms=parameters)
  out = as.data.frame(out)
  out %>% mutate(
    R_t = R0 * S,
    incid = parameters["beta"]*S*I
  )
  
}

tmp = sir_model(100, 2, 1/5)

ggplot(tmp, aes(x=time))+
  geom_line(aes(y=S,colour = "susceptible"))+
  geom_line(aes(y=I,colour = "infected"))+
  geom_line(aes(y=incid,colour = "new cases"))+
  geom_line(aes(y=R,colour = "recovered"))

ggplot(tmp, aes(x=time))+
  geom_line(
    aes(y=R_t,colour = "R_t")
    
  )

```

### Scenarios: the same epidemic at 100 different sizes

The population size `N` is swept over 100 log-spaced values from $10^{2.5}$
(about 320 people) to $10^{5}$, with ten independent replicate runs at each,
giving 1000 scenarios. Expected daily cases are `incid * N`, and the observed
counts are a binomial thinning of those at a fixed ascertainment
probability `pObs = 0.5`.

This is the key structural choice. Because the epidemic curve is identical in
shape across all 100 populations, the only thing that changes along the sweep
is the absolute number of cases, and hence the amount of information available
to the estimator in each sliding window. Peak observed case count is therefore
a clean one-dimensional measure of signal strength, and it is the x-axis of
every panel in the figure below. The ascertainment probability is held fixed
so that it does not confound that axis; the commented-out `pObs` arm is a
sensitivity check, not part of the main result.

The grouping established here — `run`, `N`, `pObs` — is carried through the
rest of the vignette. One group is one epidemic, one `EpiEstim` fit, and one
row of scores.

```{r}
scenarios = tidyr::crossing(
  N = round(10 ^ seq(2.5,5,length.out=100)),
  pObs = 0.5, #c(0.2, 0.8),
  run = 1:10
) %>% 
  dplyr::cross_join(tmp) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    cases = round(incid*N),
    obs = rbinom(dplyr::n(), cases, pObs)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(run,N,pObs) %>%
  dplyr::glimpse()

# ggplot(scenarios, aes(x=time, group=run))+
#   facet_grid(as.factor(N) ~ as.factor(pObs), scales = "free")+
#   geom_step(aes(y=obs))
  
```

## 2. Estimating $R_t$ with EpiEstim

`EpiEstim` is run once per scenario on the observed counts alone. It is given
a parametric serial interval (mean 5 days, sd 5 days), seven-day sliding
windows, and the package's own Gamma$(2,2)$ prior on $R$. It is told nothing
about the SIR model, the population size, or the ascertainment probability.

The output used here is the posterior mean and standard deviation of $R$ in
each window, which is exactly how a user of the package would report an
estimate with its uncertainty. We treat that pair as a parametrised
probabilistic prediction of $R_t$ — a Gamma distribution parametrised by mean
and standard deviation, on a log link — and score it against the true $R_t$ at
the window end. Windows with no observed cases are dropped, which is why the
number of scored predictions per scenario is itself a function of epidemic
size (a median of about 76 of the 87 windows, falling to around 46 in the
smallest epidemics).

```{r}

starts = 7:(100-7)
ends = (7+7):100
config = EpiEstim::make_config(
  method = "parametric_si",
  mean_si = 5, std_si = 5,
  t_start = starts, t_end = ends,
  mean_prior = 2, std_prior = 2
)

results = scenarios %>% dplyr::group_modify(function(d,g,...) {
  
  ee = suppressWarnings(EpiEstim::estimate_R(
    incid = data.frame(I = d$obs),
    method = "parametric_si",
    config = config,
  ))
  
  tmp = d %>% 
    filter(obs>0) %>% 
    inner_join(ee$R %>% 
                 select(time = t_end, mean=`Mean(R)`, sd = `Std(R)`), by = "time")
  return(tmp)
  
})
```


## 3. Scoring

`prediction_scores()` is applied per scenario. `max_obs`, the peak observed
case count, is computed inside the scenario grouping before the regroup, so it
indexes the scenario rather than being recomputed over a pooled set. The
threshold of 1 is the epidemiologically meaningful one: it asks how often the
prediction is on the wrong side of "the epidemic is growing".

`calibration` is `NA` here because, unlike in the synthetic experiments, there
is no injected calibration ratio to compare against — the whole point is that
the estimator's true dispersion calibration is unknown in advance and is what
the metrics are being asked to recover.

```{r}
scores = results %>% dplyr::transmute(
  max_obs = max(obs),
  true_value= R_t, location = mean, scale = sd, link="log", dist="gamma2",
  calibration=NA_real_) %>%
  group_by(max_obs, N, pObs, dist, link, calibration, run) %>%
  prediction_scores(threshold = 1) 
```

## 4. Results

```{r}

plotdata = scores %>% mutate(`P(obs)`=as.factor(pObs))

p5a = ggplot(plotdata, aes(x=max_obs, colour = `P(obs)`,y=D_pit))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE,method="loess", span=0.8)+
  scale_x_log10()+
  xlab("peak observed case count")+
  ylab("directed pit-w")
  

p5b = ggplot(plotdata, aes(x=max_obs, colour = `P(obs)`,y=U_pit))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE,method="loess", span=0.8)+
  scale_x_log10()+
  xlab("peak observed case count")+
  ylab("undirected pit-w")

p5c = ggplot(plotdata, aes(x=max_obs, colour = `P(obs)`,y=mean_crps))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE,method="loess", span=0.8)+
  scale_x_log10()+
  xlab("peak observed case count")+
  ylab("mean CRPS")

p5d = ggplot(plotdata, aes(x=max_obs, colour = `P(obs)`,y=bias))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE,method="loess", span=0.8)+
  scale_x_log10()+
  xlab("peak observed case count")+
  ylab("bias")

p5 = p5a+p5b+p5c+p5d+patchwork::plot_layout(guides="collect",axes="collect")+
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_level="A")

p5

```

### Interpretation

**$D^*_{pit}$ changes sign, and $U^*_{pit}$ is U-shaped.** Panel A shows the
directed metric rising monotonically with epidemic size and crossing zero at a
peak of roughly 56 observed cases: mean $D^*_{pit} \approx -0.079$ in the
smallest epidemics, $+0.089$ in the largest. Negative values are
under-confidence and positive values over-confidence, so `EpiEstim`'s stated
uncertainty is too wide when counts are small and too narrow when they are
large. Panel B shows the undirected metric bottoming out at a peak of around
47 cases and rising in both directions, independently locating the same sweet
spot. The two metrics are computed from different functionals of the same PIT
values, and they agree; this is the two-part diagnostic doing what it is meant
to do on data where nobody told it the answer.

**CRPS runs the other way.** Panel C falls monotonically from 0.183 to 0.087
(correlation $-0.89$ with $\log_{10}$ peak cases). Read without care it says
that the bigger the epidemic, the better the forecast. What it is actually
measuring is sharpness: in a large epidemic the posterior is narrow, so the
score is small even as calibration deteriorates. $D^*_{pit}$ is monotone in
the opposite direction (correlation $+0.91$) and is the only metric in the
panel that identifies the large-epidemic forecasts as the mis-calibrated ones.
This is the central argument of the paper, made on a real estimator rather
than a constructed example: a proper score and a dispersion diagnostic can
rank the same forecaster in opposite directions, and they are answering
different questions.

Coverage corroborates the PIT-Wasserstein reading and not the CRPS one.
Nominal 95% intervals cover 91% of true values in the smallest epidemics and
only 51% in the largest; nominal 50% intervals fall from 0.44 to 0.29. The
estimator is getting worse by the only criterion that asks whether its stated
uncertainty is honest.

**The effect sizes are large against the analytical null.** With $n$ scored
predictions per scenario, the null distributions derived in
`vignettes/significance-testing.Rmd` are $D^*_{pit} \sim N(0, 1/48n)$ and
$\mathbb{E}[U^*_{pit}] = \sqrt{2\pi}/(8\sqrt{n})$. At the median $n = 76$ that
is a null standard deviation of 0.0166 for $D^*$ and a null mean of 0.0359 for
$U^*$. Converting the binned means to those scales:

| peak observed cases | $D^*_{pit}$ z-score | $U^*_{pit}$ / null mean |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | $-3.7$ | 1.8 |
| 18 | $-2.5$ | 1.4 |
| 36 | $-1.0$ | 1.3 |
| 73 | $+0.7$ | 1.5 |
| 148 | $+1.8$ | 1.9 |
| 304 | $+3.1$ | 2.2 |
| 617 | $+4.4$ | 2.6 |
| 1261 | $+5.7$ | 3.0 |

Only the band around 36–73 peak cases is statistically indistinguishable from
calibrated. Note that these are analytical critical values, not a simulated
reference table: the real-data example exercises the theory rather than merely
illustrating the metric.

**Bias is present throughout and does not contaminate the dispersion
verdict.** Panel D shows a systematic negative bias at every epidemic size
($-0.185$ falling to $-0.088$): `EpiEstim`'s $R_t$ sits above the truth,
plausibly a combination of the Gamma$(2,2)$ prior pulling towards 2 and the
seven-day window lagging a falling $R_t$. The unadjusted undirected metric
`U_pit_unadj` sits between 0.24 and 0.30 and is nearly flat, while the
bias-adjusted `U_pit` sits between 0.05 and 0.10 and carries all the
structure. Almost all of the raw PIT deviation is location error; the
adjustment removes it and leaves the dispersion signal, which is the
invariance property claimed for the metrics, demonstrated here on an error
nobody designed.

### Caveats

This experiment identifies *that* the dispersion calibration changes sign with
epidemic size; it does not separate the contributions of the Gamma prior, the
window width, and any genuine over-confidence in the renewal-equation
likelihood. Disentangling those would need a prior and window-width
sensitivity sweep and is out of scope here. `pObs` is fixed at 0.5, so the
`P(obs)` colour aesthetic currently has a single level.

```{r}

.gg_save_as(
  p5,
  file.path(fig_dir, "fig5-epiestim-by-epi-size"),
  size = std_size$two_third,
  formats = c("pdf", "eps")
)

```
